excerpt: Planning a Mt Longonot hike? Here is the route, honest timings, getting there from Nairobi, what to pack and how to stay safe on the crater rim.
content:
The Mt Longonot hike is one of the most rewarding day trips you can do from Nairobi, and one of the most underestimated. On a map it looks short and simple, but the dusty volcanic slopes, the steep climb to the rim and the exposed loop around the crater catch out plenty of first-timers every weekend.

This guide gives you everything you need to plan the day well: how to get there, the route in stages, honest timings, the gear that makes a real difference, and the safety points that keep a great day from turning into a long one. Whether you are going solo, with friends or with a guided group, you will know exactly what to expect.

Mt Longonot Hike: Quick Facts

  • Location: Mount Longonot National Park, about 60 km north-west of Nairobi, near Naivasha
  • Summit height: 2,776 m above sea level; the gate sits at roughly 2,150 m
  • Gate to crater rim: about 3.1 km
  • Crater rim loop: about 7.2 km
  • Full circuit (gate, rim loop and back): about 13.5 km, usually 4 to 6 hours
  • Difficulty: moderate to challenging, with steep, loose and dusty sections
  • Managed by: Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS); confirm current entry fees with KWS before you go

What Makes the Mt Longonot Hike Special

Mount Longonot is a dormant stratovolcano rising above the floor of the Great Rift Valley. Its last eruption is thought to have happened in the 1860s, which is recent in geological terms, and the mountain still looks raw. The summit cone is crowned by a wide crater roughly 1.8 km across, its floor covered in thick forest that you look down on for most of the loop.

What sets the Mt Longonot hike apart from other hikes near Nairobi is the variety packed into one day. You start in open grassland where you may spot zebra, giraffe, Thomson's gazelle, hartebeest or buffalo, then climb onto ash ridges with sweeping views of Lake Naivasha and the Rift Valley floor. Few day hikes in Kenya give you a volcano, wildlife and a lake view all at once.

Many Kenyan hikers use the Mt Longonot hike as a training benchmark before bigger objectives such as Mt Kenya or the Aberdares, because the climbing is steep and sustained without needing an overnight stay.

Getting to Mount Longonot National Park

The park lies about 60 km from Nairobi, so most people heading out for a Mt Longonot hike drive out early in the morning. Leaving the city before 6:00 am gets you ahead of the traffic on the escarpment and lets you start walking while it is still cool.

By car

Take the road down the escarpment towards Mai Mahiu and on towards Naivasha. At Longonot Centre, turn off near the railway bridge and follow the signposted dirt track that runs alongside the railway line. The park gate is roughly 4 km from the turn-off. The track is usually fine for ordinary cars in dry weather but can turn muddy and rutted after heavy rain.

By public transport

Matatus to Naivasha leave from the River Road area in Nairobi. From Naivasha, catch a vehicle heading towards Mai Mahiu and get off at Longonot. Boda bodas wait in the centre and can take you the last few kilometres to the gate. Agree on the fare before you set off.

Entry fees and payment

Fees change from time to time and differ for citizens, residents and non-residents, so check the latest rates directly with Kenya Wildlife Service before you travel. Have M-Pesa ready and confirm which payment methods the gate currently accepts, as KWS has been moving parks towards cashless payment.

The Mt Longonot Hike Route, Stage by Stage

The Mt Longonot hike route is clear and well used, so navigation is easy in good visibility. The challenge is the terrain: fine volcanic dust, loose gravel and steep steps where the path has eroded. Here is how the day usually unfolds.

Stage 1: Gate to the crater rim (about 3.1 km)

From the gate, the path starts gently through grassland and scattered trees, then steepens steadily. The final section up to the rim is the hardest part of the ascent, with deep gullies and loose ground that slides underfoot. Most hikers reach the rim in 1 to 1.5 hours. Take short, steady steps and enjoy the views back over the valley.

Stage 2: The crater rim loop (about 7.2 km)

Once you reach the rim, you can decide whether to turn back or commit to the full loop. Going clockwise, the path climbs to the true summit at 2,776 m, the highest point of the Mt Longonot hike. This section has some narrow, exposed stretches with steep drops on either side, so watch your footing, especially in wind. After the summit, the trail rolls up and down around the crater before returning to where you joined the rim. Allow 2 to 3 hours for the loop.

Stage 3: Descent to the gate

The way down follows the same path you came up. It is shorter in time, often about an hour, but it is where many slips happen. Loose dust acts like ball bearings on steep ground, and tired legs make mistakes. Slow down, keep your weight over your feet and use trekking poles if you have them.

Rim only or the full loop?

If you are new to hiking, short on time or the weather is turning, going up to the rim and back is still a satisfying outing of about 6 km. Fit hikers who start early should aim for the full circuit, as the summit and the far side of the crater are the highlights.

Best Time for a Mt Longonot Hike

Kenya's long rains usually fall from about March to May, and the short rains from about October to December. During these months the ash trail can become slick and muddy, gullies channel running water, and afternoon storms roll in quickly. The drier months, roughly January to February and June to September, generally give firmer footing and clearer views.

The dry season brings its own challenge: dust. In a dry spell the trail turns to powder, and the sun on the exposed rim can be fierce, as there is little shade once you leave the lower slopes. Whatever the month, start between 7:00 and 9:00 am so you finish the steep sections before the midday heat and before any afternoon rain.

Weekends and public holidays are busy, especially on the climb to the rim. If you prefer a quieter trail, a weekday visit is worth considering.

What to Pack for the Mt Longonot Hike

Good gear does not need to be expensive. All of our kit is quality thrifted gear, carefully checked and priced so that reliable, proper hiking equipment is within reach of every Kenyan hiker. Here is what we recommend for the Mt Longonot hike.

Footwear and socks

Boots or trail shoes with deep tread and solid ankle support are the single most important item for a Mt Longonot hike. A pair like the Quechua Waterproof Hiking Boot grips the loose ash well and keeps dust and grit out better than running shoes. Pair them with cushioned Merino Wool Hiking Socks, which manage sweat and help prevent blisters on the steep descent.

Water and a comfortable pack

There is no drinking water along the Mt Longonot hike route, so carry at least 2 to 3 litres per person, more on hot days or if you plan the full loop. A hydration pack such as the 3L Camel Hydration Backpack lets you sip on the move without stopping. If you prefer bottles, a roomy 28L Day Hiking Backpack fits water, snacks, a warm layer and a rain jacket with room to spare.

Sun and weather protection

The rim is high and exposed, so pack a wide-brimmed hat, sunscreen and good sunglasses with UV400 lenses, which also help keep blowing dust out of your eyes. A light windproof or rain jacket is wise in every season, because the weather on top can change quickly.

Small extras that help

  • Buff or bandana: pull it over your nose and mouth on dusty sections.
  • Trekking poles: they take strain off your knees on the descent.
  • Energy snacks: nuts, fruit, groundnuts or energy bars for the rim.
  • Small first-aid kit: plasters, blister patches and any personal medication.
  • Rubbish bag: carry out everything you carry in.

Safety Tips for Your Mt Longonot Hike

Longonot is a well-managed park and generally a safe place to hike, but every Mt Longonot hike deserves respect. Most problems on the mountain come from dehydration, slips on loose ground and people pushing on when they should turn back.

Wildlife

There are no lions or elephants in the park, but buffalo do live here and should never be approached. If you see one, give it plenty of space and let it move off. Baboons may also appear near rest spots; keep food packed away and never feed them.

Pacing and turnaround time

Set a turnaround time before you start. If you have not reached the rim by late morning, or clouds and thunder are building, it is sensible to skip the full loop. The exposed summit ridge is no place to be in a lightning storm or strong wind.

Know your limits

Take regular short breaks, drink little and often, and eat before you feel hungry. Children who are active and used to walking can often manage the climb to the rim with close supervision, but the full loop is a big day for young legs.

Pro Tips for the Mt Longonot Hike

  • Leave Nairobi before 6:00 am and start walking by 8:00 am at the latest.
  • Use the toilets at the gate before you set off; there are none on the trail.
  • Carry at least 2 to 3 litres of water each, as there is none to refill along the route.
  • Wear boots with deep tread, and slow right down on the dusty descent.
  • Keep a buff handy for dust and a light jacket for wind on the rim.
  • Agree on a turnaround time and stick to it if the weather changes.
  • Stay on the marked path and pack out all your litter.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does the Mt Longonot hike take?

Most hikers need 4 to 6 hours for a full Mt Longonot hike circuit of about 13.5 km, including breaks. Going from the gate to the rim and back, without the loop, usually takes 2 to 3 hours.

Is the Mt Longonot hike suitable for beginners?

Yes, with the right preparation. Beginners with reasonable fitness can reach the rim, and many complete the full loop by starting early and pacing themselves. The terrain is steep and loose, so good shoes and plenty of water matter more than speed.

Can I do the Mt Longonot hike in the rainy season?

You can, but expect slippery ash, muddy gullies and a higher chance of afternoon storms during the long rains (around March to May) and the short rains (around October to December). Start early, wear boots with good grip and be ready to turn back at the rim.

Is there water or food in the park?

No. There is no drinking water on the trail and no food for sale along the route, so carry everything you need for the day. Basic facilities are only available near the gate.

Do I need a guide to hike Mount Longonot?

A guide is not required, as the trail is clear and well used. Many first-timers still prefer to hike with a guide or an organised group for company, local knowledge and help with transport.

Final Thoughts

The Mt Longonot hike rewards anyone who prepares for it: steep ash slopes, a dramatic crater and some of the best views in the Rift Valley, all within easy reach of Nairobi. Start early, carry plenty of water, wear boots that grip and take the descent slowly, and you will come home tired, dusty and very happy. Pick your date, check your gear, and get out on the rim.
